description: The party staple. Rice cooked in a fried pepper-and-tomato base until every grain takes the colour, finished low and slow so the bottom catches just enough.
name: Jollof Rice

steps.heading: Blend the base
steps.description: Blend the tomatoes, tatashe, scotch bonnet and one onion until smooth. Do not add water — the tomatoes carry enough of their own.

steps.heading: Reduce the blend
steps.description: Pour the blend into a dry pot and boil it down until the water is gone and it thickens. Skipping this is why jollof turns out watery.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Heat the oil, slice in the second onion and fry until translucent. Add the tomato paste and fry two minutes, then the reduced blend. Fry until the oil separates and floats to the top and the raw smell is gone. This is the step that makes it jollof.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Stir in the stock cubes, thyme, curry and bay leaves. Taste it now — this is the last easy moment to fix the salt.

steps.heading: Add the rice
steps.description: Wash the rice until the water runs clear, then stir it into the base. Add water until it sits level with the rice, not above it.

steps.heading: Steam it down
steps.description: Cover tightly, lowest heat. Do not stir and do not lift the lid for twenty minutes. Foil under the lid helps if yours does not seal.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Check a grain. If it needs more, sprinkle a little hot water at the edges and cover again. Take it off, leave it five minutes, then stir from the bottom up.

whatMakesItGood: The smoky bottom. Jollof lives or dies on how long you fry the base before the rice goes in — rush it and you get red rice, take your time and you get jollof.

description: Ground melon seed cooked in palm oil until it lumps and thickens, with leafy greens and whatever meat is in the house.
name: Egusi Soup

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Season the beef and ponmo with onion, one stock cube and salt. Cook covered in its own liquid until tender, adding water only if it threatens to burn. Keep the stock.

steps.heading: Fry the egusi
steps.description: Heat the palm oil until it thins but does not smoke. Stir the ground egusi into a thick paste with a little stock, drop it in spoonfuls, and let it fry without stirring until the lumps set.

steps.heading: Build the soup
steps.description: Pour in the reserved stock a little at a time so the lumps stay whole. Add the blended pepper, crayfish, iru and the dried fish.

steps.heading: Simmer
steps.description: Cover and let it cook until the oil rises to the top. Taste for salt.

steps.heading: Add the greens
steps.description: Stir in the ugu and take it off the heat almost immediately — the residual heat is enough, and a boiled leaf loses its bite.

whatMakesItGood: The lumps. Egusi fried properly holds together in soft clumps rather than dissolving into a paste — that texture is the whole point, and it comes from frying it in the oil before any water goes near it.

description: A Yoruba vegetable stew where the greens are the point, not a garnish — cooked in a fried pepper base with iru and assorted meat.
name: Efo Riro

steps.heading: Prepare the greens
steps.description: Wash the spinach well, slice it, and squeeze out as much water as you can. Wet greens water down the whole pot.

steps.heading: Blend the pepper
steps.description: Roughly blend the tatashe, scotch bonnet and half the onion. Leave it coarse — efo riro wants texture, not a smooth sauce.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Heat the palm oil, fry the remaining sliced onion, then add the pepper blend. Fry until it darkens and the oil separates.

steps.heading: Add the flavour
steps.description: Stir in iru, crayfish, stock cubes and the dried fish, plus the meat and its stock if you are using it. Simmer.

steps.heading: Fold in the greens
steps.description: Add the squeezed spinach and fold rather than stir. Two minutes on the heat, no more, then off.

whatMakesItGood: The pepper base is fried down hard before the greens go in, so the vegetables stay bright and firm rather than stewing into mush.

description: Local unpolished rice with the green pepper sauce known as designer stew — bleached palm oil, green peppers, and assorted meat.
name: Ofada Rice and Ayamase

steps.heading: Cook the meats
steps.description: Season and boil the beef, shaki and ponmo separately until each is tender — they take very different times. Keep every drop of the stock.

steps.heading: Blend the peppers
steps.description: Blend the green chillies, bell peppers and one onion coarsely, then boil the blend down until almost dry.

steps.heading: Bleach the oil
steps.description: Heat the palm oil on medium until it stops smoking heavily and turns clear. Open a window. This is what makes it ayamase and there is no shortcut.

steps.heading: Fry the sauce
steps.description: Fry the second onion in the bleached oil, add iru, then the reduced pepper. Fry until the oil floats clear on top.

steps.heading: Finish the sauce
steps.description: Add the meats, crayfish, stock cubes and enough stock to loosen it. Simmer, then fold in halved boiled eggs.

steps.heading: Cook the rice
steps.description: Parboil the ofada rice, rinse it well to take the local edge off, then steam until tender. Serve in the leaves if you have them.

whatMakesItGood: The bleached palm oil. Heating the oil until it turns clear is what gives ayamase its particular smoky depth, and nothing else substitutes for it.

description: Soft brown beans cooked down with palm oil and pepper, served with sweet fried plantain.
name: Beans and Fried Plantain

steps.heading: Boil the beans
steps.description: Pick over the beans, rinse, and boil in plenty of water. Do not salt yet — salt early keeps beans hard.

steps.heading: Check for softness
steps.description: A bean should crush easily between two fingers. If the water runs low top it up with hot, never cold — cold water shocks them firm.

steps.heading: Season it down
steps.description: Drain most of the water. Stir in palm oil, sliced onion, blended pepper, crayfish, stock cubes and salt. Let it thicken.

steps.heading: Fry the plantain
steps.description: Slice the plantain on the diagonal, fry in hot oil until each side is deep gold, and drain on paper.

whatMakesItGood: The contrast. Savoury, slightly smoky beans against plantain fried until the sugars catch — it is the cheapest complete meal in the country and one of the best.

description: Beans mashed down to a soft paste, served with the near-black fried pepper sauce that gives it its name.
name: Ewa Agoyin

steps.heading: Cook the beans soft
steps.description: Boil the beans until they are past tender and starting to break apart. Ewa agoyin wants them mashed, so overcooking is the goal.

steps.heading: Mash
steps.description: Mash them roughly with a wooden spoon. Some texture left is fine.

steps.heading: Fry the onions
steps.description: Slice the onions thin and fry slowly in the palm oil until they go from soft to brown to almost black. This takes far longer than feels right. Do not rush it.

steps.heading: Finish the sauce
steps.description: Stir in the dry pepper and stock cubes, fry two more minutes, then take it off. Spoon over the beans.

whatMakesItGood: The sauce. Onions and dried pepper fried in palm oil far past the point you would think sensible, until it goes dark, sweet and slightly bitter.

description: Steamed bean pudding — peeled beans blended with pepper and onion, then steamed in leaves until set.
name: Moin Moin

steps.heading: Peel the beans
steps.description: Soak the beans twenty minutes, then rub between your palms until the skins float off. Rinse them away. This is tedious and there is no way around it.

steps.heading: Blend thick
steps.description: Blend the peeled beans with pepper and onion using as little water as you can. A watery blend will never set.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Stir in oil, crayfish, stock cubes and salt. Beat it with a spoon for a minute — it lightens the texture.

steps.heading: Fill and steam
steps.description: Line the moulds with leaves, pour in the mix, tuck in egg if using. Steam upright with water halfway up the moulds.

steps.heading: Test
steps.description: A knife should come out clean. If not, steam ten more minutes and check again.

whatMakesItGood: The texture when it is right: soft and set, never dense. Blending with as little water as possible is the whole trick.

description: A thin, fiercely aromatic broth with fresh catfish, scent leaf and pepper soup spice.
name: Catfish Pepper Soup

steps.heading: Clean the fish
steps.description: Wash the catfish with hot water and a little salt or lime to take off the slime. Cut into steaks.

steps.heading: Build the broth
steps.description: Bring water to the boil with blended onion and pepper, the pepper soup spice and stock cubes.

steps.heading: Add the fish
steps.description: Slide the fish in gently and do not stir — catfish falls apart. Shake the pot instead.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Drop in the scent leaf and uziza in the last two minutes, take it off, and let it sit briefly before serving.

whatMakesItGood: It is medicine as much as food. Hot, clear and aromatic — the thing you want when it rains or when you are unwell.

description: The drawing soup — ground bush mango seed cooked in palm oil until it pulls into long threads.
name: Ogbono Soup

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Season and cook the beef until tender. Reserve the stock — it carries the whole soup.

steps.heading: Dissolve the ogbono
steps.description: Warm the palm oil on low and stir the ground ogbono into it until it dissolves completely and starts to draw. Never add it straight to water or it will clump and never recover.

steps.heading: Loosen with stock
steps.description: Add the stock little by little, stirring constantly. Too fast and the draw breaks.

steps.heading: Simmer
steps.description: Add crayfish, dried fish, pepper and stock cubes. Simmer uncovered — covering it kills the draw.

steps.heading: Add the greens
steps.description: Stir in the ugu, one minute, then off the heat.

whatMakesItGood: The draw. Ogbono is judged entirely on how far it stretches from the plate, and that comes from dissolving it in the oil before any water touches it.

description: Rice fried with curry, liver and diced vegetables — green, aromatic, and nothing like the Chinese dish it borrows its name from.
name: Nigerian Fried Rice

steps.heading: Parboil the rice
steps.description: Parboil the rice until just short of done, then rinse in cold water and drain completely. Wet rice will steam instead of fry.

steps.heading: Make the stock
steps.description: Boil the liver with onion, thyme and a stock cube. Dice it small and keep the stock.

steps.heading: Cook the rice in stock
steps.description: Return the rice to the pot with the curry and just enough stock to colour it. Steam until done but still firm.

steps.heading: Fry the vegetables
steps.description: On high heat, fry the diced carrots, beans and peas hard and fast — two minutes, no more. They must stay crunchy.

steps.heading: Bring it together
steps.description: Fold the vegetables and liver through the rice off the heat. Taste, adjust, serve.

whatMakesItGood: The curry-stained rice and the crunch of vegetables that were barely cooked. It is a party dish that lives or dies on not overcooking anything.

description: Yam cooked down in a palm oil and pepper base until it half-collapses into its own sauce.
name: Asaro (Yam Porridge)

steps.heading: Prepare the yam
steps.description: Peel and cube the yam, rinse, and put it in a pot with water just below the top of the yam.

steps.heading: Boil with the base
steps.description: Add blended pepper, onion, palm oil, crayfish and stock cubes. Boil covered until the yam softens.

steps.heading: Break it down
steps.description: Mash about half the yam against the side of the pot and stir. The rest stays in pieces.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add the dried fish and the ugu, cook two more minutes, and take it off before the leaves go dull.

whatMakesItGood: You want it partly mashed and partly whole — some pieces holding their shape, the rest breaking down to thicken the pot.

description: Chopped okra cooked briefly so it keeps its draw and its bite, with palm oil, crayfish and fish.
name: Okra Soup

steps.heading: Chop the okra
steps.description: Chop it fine by hand for more draw, or grate it coarsely for texture. Do not blend — blending destroys it.

steps.heading: Start the base
steps.description: Bring stock, palm oil, blended pepper, crayfish, dried fish and stock cubes to a simmer.

steps.heading: Add the okra
steps.description: Stir in the okra and cook no more than five minutes. It should still be bright green.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Fold in the ugu if using, taste for salt, and take it straight off the heat.

whatMakesItGood: Speed. Okra cooked more than a few minutes goes slimy and dull — in and out fast is the entire technique.

description: The red stew that goes with everything — rice, yam, beans, bread. Fried pepper base with browned chicken.
name: Nigerian Chicken Stew

steps.heading: Season and boil
steps.description: Season the chicken with onion, thyme, curry, a stock cube and salt. Boil in its own moisture until cooked. Keep the stock.

steps.heading: Fry the chicken
steps.description: Fry the pieces until golden. This is optional but it changes the dish.

steps.heading: Reduce the blend
steps.description: Blend tomatoes, tatashe, scotch bonnet and one onion, then boil it down until thick.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry sliced onion in the oil, add tomato paste, then the reduced blend. Fry until the oil floats clear on top.

steps.heading: Bring together
steps.description: Add the chicken and enough stock to loosen. Simmer twenty minutes so the flavours settle.

whatMakesItGood: It is the backbone of Nigerian cooking. Made properly it keeps for days and gets better, and it is the base for half the other dishes in the house.

description: Gizzard and fried plantain tossed in a thick pepper sauce. A party plate that works as a full meal.
name: Gizdodo

steps.heading: Cook the gizzard
steps.description: Boil the gizzard with onion, curry, stock cube and salt until tender. It takes longer than you expect.

steps.heading: Fry separately
steps.description: Fry the gizzard until the edges crisp. Fry the diced plantain until deep gold. Keep them apart.

steps.heading: Make the sauce
steps.description: Fry blended tatashe and scotch bonnet in a little oil until thick and the oil separates.

steps.heading: Toss
steps.description: Off the heat, fold the gizzard and plantain through the sauce so both are coated but neither breaks.

whatMakesItGood: Chewy gizzard against sweet plantain in a sauce thick enough to coat both. Everything must be fried separately or it turns to mush.

description: Instant noodles cooked the way every Nigerian student learns to — with egg, vegetables and far more pepper than the packet suggests.
name: Nigerian Indomie Stir-fry

steps.heading: Boil the noodles
steps.description: Boil for three minutes only — they will cook further in the pan. Drain and keep a splash of the water.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry sliced onion, pepper, carrot and cabbage on high heat for two minutes. Keep them crunchy.

steps.heading: Scramble the egg
steps.description: Push the vegetables aside, scramble the eggs in the same pan, then mix through.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add the noodles, both sachets, and a splash of the reserved water. Toss until everything is coated.

whatMakesItGood: Fifteen minutes, almost no skill, and it tastes far better than the sum of what goes into it.

description: Boiled yam with a loose tomato and egg sauce. The default Nigerian breakfast when there is yam in the house.
name: Boiled Yam and Egg Sauce

steps.heading: Boil the yam
steps.description: Peel, cut into rounds, and boil in salted water until a knife slides in easily.

steps.heading: Fry the sauce
steps.description: Fry sliced onion, then chopped tomato and pepper, until the water cooks off and it thickens.

steps.heading: Add the eggs
steps.description: Beat the eggs, pour them in, and stir slowly so you get soft folds rather than a scramble.

whatMakesItGood: Twenty minutes from nothing to a full meal, using things almost every kitchen already has.

description: Peeled beans blended and deep fried into light, airy fritters. Breakfast, usually with pap.
name: Akara

steps.heading: Peel the beans
steps.description: Soak twenty minutes and rub off the skins. Rinse them away completely — any skin left shows in the finished akara.

steps.heading: Blend thick
steps.description: Blend with almost no water, plus the onion and pepper. A runny batter will not hold.

steps.heading: Beat it
steps.description: Beat the batter hard with a wooden spoon for several minutes until it lightens and holds air. This is what makes them puff.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Drop spoonfuls into hot oil. They should float and turn quickly. Fry until deep gold and drain.

whatMakesItGood: When the batter is beaten properly they puff hollow and light. A dense akara means it was not beaten enough.

description: Thin beef coated in spiced groundnut mix and grilled hard over open heat.
name: Suya

steps.heading: Slice thin
steps.description: Slice the beef as thin as you can across the grain. Thick suya is tough suya.

steps.heading: Coat
steps.description: Rub the meat with oil, then press the suya spice on hard so it sticks. Rest it thirty minutes if you have time.

steps.heading: Skewer and grill
steps.description: Thread onto skewers and grill close to high heat, turning often, until the edges char.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Dust with more spice off the heat and serve with raw onion, cabbage and tomato.

whatMakesItGood: The yaji. Groundnut, pepper and spice crusted onto the meat and toasted by the fire — it is the coating, not the beef, that people queue for.

description: Delta palm fruit soup — rich, oily and heavily spiced, usually with fresh fish or beef.
name: Banga Soup

steps.heading: Prepare the base
steps.description: Pour the palm fruit concentrate into a pot with water and bring to a boil.

steps.heading: Reduce
steps.description: Let it boil down uncovered until it thickens noticeably and the oil starts to show.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Add banga spice, crayfish, blended pepper, onion and stock cubes.

steps.heading: Add the fish
steps.description: Slide in the catfish and do not stir — shake the pot instead. Simmer until cooked through.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Scent leaf goes in at the very end, off the heat.

whatMakesItGood: The palm fruit concentrate gives a depth nothing else does, and the banga spice mix is unlike any other Nigerian soup.

description: Efik soup of ground okazi leaf and waterleaf, thick with meat and dried fish.
name: Afang Soup

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Cook the beef and ponmo with onion and stock cube until tender. Keep the stock.

steps.heading: Prepare the leaves
steps.description: Pound or blend the afang leaves coarsely. Slice the waterleaf and squeeze out excess water.

steps.heading: Build
steps.description: Add palm oil, crayfish, pepper and dried fish to the meat and stock. Simmer.

steps.heading: Add waterleaf
steps.description: Stir in the waterleaf first and let it cook down — it releases liquid the afang will absorb.

steps.heading: Add afang
steps.description: Stir in the afang last, cook five minutes, and take it off. It should be thick, not watery.

whatMakesItGood: The balance of two leaves: waterleaf brings the moisture, okazi brings the body. Neither works alone.

description: The Yoruba pairing — smooth jute leaf soup alongside a bean soup, both spooned over amala with stew.
name: Ewedu and Gbegiri

steps.heading: Cook the gbegiri
steps.description: Boil the beans until completely soft, then sieve or blend and pass through to remove the skins. It should be smooth and pourable.

steps.heading: Season the gbegiri
steps.description: Return to the pot with palm oil, crayfish and stock cube. Simmer until it thickens slightly.

steps.heading: Cook the ewedu
steps.description: Boil the ewedu leaves with a little potash and iru, then blend with a broom or blender until smooth and drawing.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Season the ewedu with crayfish and stock cube. Serve both alongside amala and stew.

whatMakesItGood: Three things on one plate that make no sense alone and complete each other together. Abula, properly.

description: Rice cooked in coconut milk with pepper and vegetables — sweeter and softer than jollof.
name: Coconut Rice

steps.heading: Blend and reduce
steps.description: Blend tomatoes, tatashe, pepper and half the onion, then boil down until thick.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry the remaining onion in oil, add the reduced blend, and fry until the oil separates.

steps.heading: Add coconut milk
steps.description: Pour in the coconut milk and stock cubes, bring to a simmer.

steps.heading: Cook the rice
steps.description: Stir in washed rice, cover tightly and cook on low. Add hot water only if it dries before the rice softens.

steps.heading: Rest
steps.description: Off the heat, leave covered five minutes, then fold through the diced carrots.

whatMakesItGood: Coconut milk instead of water changes everything: the rice comes out richer and slightly sweet, and it needs far less seasoning.

description: Unripe plantain cooked down in a palm oil base with greens until thick and soft.
name: Plantain Porridge

steps.heading: Prepare the plantain
steps.description: Peel and cube the unripe plantain. Keep it in water until you are ready or it darkens.

steps.heading: Boil with the base
steps.description: Cook with blended pepper, onion, palm oil, crayfish and stock cubes, water just below the top.

steps.heading: Thicken
steps.description: Mash a few pieces against the pot to thicken the sauce, leaving most whole.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add dried fish and ugu, two more minutes, off the heat.

whatMakesItGood: Unripe plantain holds shape better than yam and brings a firmness porridge otherwise lacks. A good one-pot when there is little in the house.

description: Spaghetti cooked directly in a jollof base so it absorbs the sauce instead of sitting under it.
name: Spaghetti Jollof

steps.heading: Make the base
steps.description: Blend and reduce the tomatoes, tatashe and pepper, then fry with onion, paste and oil until the oil separates.

steps.heading: Loosen
steps.description: Add water or stock — roughly enough to cook the pasta — plus stock cubes and curry.

steps.heading: Cook the pasta in it
steps.description: Break the spaghetti in, stir once, cover and simmer. Stir occasionally so it does not catch.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: When the pasta is done the sauce should be almost gone. Fold in sliced sausage if using.

whatMakesItGood: Cooking the pasta in the sauce rather than boiling it separately — every strand takes the colour and the pepper.

name: Ofe Nsala (White Soup)
whatMakesItGood: It is the only Nigerian soup that gets its body from pounded yam rather than seeds or oil, which is why it tastes clean instead of heavy. Traditionally the soup for a new mother.
description: The white soup — no palm oil, no tomato. Catfish and yam thickener carry it, and uziza gives the lift.

steps.heading: Clean the fish
steps.description: Wash the catfish with hot water and a little salt to firm the skin, so it does not fall apart in the pot.

steps.heading: Boil the yam
steps.description: Boil the yam pieces until very soft, then pound or blend a little water into a smooth paste. This is the thickener.

steps.heading: Start the pot
steps.description: Put the fish in a pot with the crayfish, ground scotch bonnet, uda, stock cubes and just enough water to cover. Simmer gently.

steps.heading: Thicken
steps.description: Drop the yam paste in small lumps into the simmering pot. Do not stir hard — let each lump dissolve on its own or the soup goes gluey.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add the uziza and utazi, taste for salt, and take it off after two minutes. The leaves should still be green.

name: Oha Soup
whatMakesItGood: Oha leaves are torn, not sliced, because the metal bruises them and they blacken. That one detail is the difference between a green soup and a grey one.
description: Cocoyam-thickened soup with oha leaves torn by hand, never cut — a knife turns them dark.

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Boil the beef and stockfish with one stock cube, onion and salt until tender. Keep every drop of the stock.

steps.heading: Prepare the cocoyam
steps.description: Boil the cocoyam until soft, peel, and pound to a smooth lump-free paste.

steps.heading: Build the soup
steps.description: Add the dried fish, crayfish, ground pepper and iru to the meat stock and let it come to a boil.

steps.heading: Thicken
steps.description: Drop the cocoyam paste in small lumps. Cover and let it dissolve without stirring for five minutes, then stir once.

steps.heading: Add oha
steps.description: Pour in the palm oil, then tear the oha leaves in by hand and turn off the heat after two minutes.

name: Edikang Ikong
whatMakesItGood: It is a vegetable soup where the vegetables are the point, not a garnish. Waterleaf releases the moisture that cooks the ugu, which is why you add almost no water at all.
description: The Calabar vegetable soup — far more leaf than liquid, with ugu and waterleaf in a ratio that looks like too much until it wilts.

steps.heading: Cook the meats
steps.description: Boil the beef, ponmo and stockfish together with stock cubes and onion until tender. Reduce the stock right down — this soup must not be watery.

steps.heading: Wash the leaves
steps.description: Wash and slice the ugu and waterleaf separately. Keep them apart; they go in at different times.

steps.heading: Add oil and fish
steps.description: Stir the palm oil, crayfish, ground pepper and dried fish into the reduced stock and simmer.

steps.heading: Waterleaf first
steps.description: Add the waterleaf and let it wilt down. It will release a lot of liquid — let that boil off before the next step.

steps.heading: Ugu last
steps.description: Stir in the ugu and the periwinkle, cover for three minutes, and turn it off. The ugu should still be bright.

name: Banga Soup with Atama
whatMakesItGood: The same palm base as banga, but atama instead of scent leaf changes it completely. It is bitter in the way good things are.
description: Palm fruit soup finished with atama leaf — the Efik reading of banga, thinner than the Delta version and more aromatic.

steps.heading: Boil the meat
steps.description: Cook the beef and ponmo with stock cubes and salt until tender.

steps.heading: Add the palm base
steps.description: Pour the palm fruit concentrate over the meat and bring it to a rolling boil. Do not cover it — it needs to reduce.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Add the dried fish, crayfish and ground pepper. Simmer until the oil begins to rise to the surface.

steps.heading: Finish with leaves
steps.description: Stir in the scent leaf, check the salt, and turn off after two minutes.

name: Gbegiri
whatMakesItGood: Everything depends on sieving. A gbegiri with skins in it is just bean porridge — the silk texture is the whole dish.
description: Smooth brown-bean soup, sieved until there is not a single skin left. Half of the abula pairing.

steps.heading: Soak and peel
steps.description: Soak the beans for an hour, then rub them between your palms until the skins float off. Rinse the skins away completely.

steps.heading: Boil soft
steps.description: Boil the peeled beans with onion until they collapse entirely — well past tender.

steps.heading: Sieve
steps.description: Mash and push everything through a sieve. This is the step that cannot be skipped.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Return the smooth paste to the pot with palm oil, crayfish, pepper and stock cubes. Whisk as it heats so it does not catch.

name: Ofe Akwu (Palm Nut Stew)
whatMakesItGood: Banga and ofe akwu start from the same palm concentrate, but this one is thinned and served over rice. Cheaper than a tomato stew when tomatoes are expensive.
description: Palm fruit stew eaten with white rice rather than swallow — lighter than banga, and the everyday Sunday version.

steps.heading: Cook the beef
steps.description: Boil the beef with onion, one stock cube and salt until tender, keeping the stock.

steps.heading: Reduce the palm
steps.description: Add the palm concentrate to the meat and stock, and boil uncovered until it thickens and the oil separates out.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Stir in crayfish, ground pepper, dried fish and the rest of the stock cubes. Simmer.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add scent leaf, taste, and take it off the heat. Serve over white rice.

name: Ogbono and Okra Mix
whatMakesItGood: Ogbono alone can go slimy in a heavy way; the okra lightens it and adds bite. This is the compromise version everybody's mother makes.
description: Ogbono drawn with okra stirred through — twice the draw, and the combination most people actually cook at home.

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Boil the beef and ponmo with a stock cube and onion until tender. Keep the stock.

steps.heading: Dissolve the ogbono
steps.description: Melt the palm oil on low heat, take it off, and stir the ground ogbono into the warm oil until it is a smooth paste with no lumps.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add the ogbono paste to the boiling meat stock, stirring so it does not clump. Let it draw for five minutes.

steps.heading: Add okra
steps.description: Grate or chop the okra in, along with the crayfish, pepper and dried fish. Do not overcook or the okra loses its draw.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Stir in the ugu, check the salt, and serve immediately.

name: Fisherman Soup
whatMakesItGood: It is a soup where the seafood is not an addition but the whole cast. Because nothing is fried first, you taste the water, not the oil.
description: Everything from the water in one pot — fresh fish, prawns, periwinkle — in a light peppery broth.

steps.heading: Clean everything
steps.description: Wash the catfish in hot salted water, rinse the prawns and periwinkle well. Grit ruins this soup.

steps.heading: Build the broth
steps.description: Bring water, ground pepper, crayfish, stock cubes and palm oil to a boil and let the flavours come together before any fish goes in.

steps.heading: Add the seafood
steps.description: Slide in the catfish first, then the periwinkle. Simmer gently — do not stir, or the fish breaks up.

steps.heading: Prawns last
steps.description: Add the prawns and uziza in the final three minutes. Prawns need almost no time and turn rubbery if you give them more.

steps.heading: Rest
steps.description: Take it off and let it sit for five minutes before serving so the broth settles.

name: Groundnut Soup
whatMakesItGood: Groundnut paste does the thickening and the seasoning at once. It is the closest Nigerian soup to a West African maafe, and it fills you up on very little meat.
description: Peanut-thickened soup, rich and slightly sweet, common across the north and into the middle belt.

steps.heading: Cook the beef
steps.description: Boil the beef with onion, stock cube and salt until tender. Reserve the stock.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Blend the tomatoes, pepper and remaining onion and fry in the oil until the raw smell goes.

steps.heading: Loosen the paste
steps.description: Mix the groundnut paste with a ladle of hot stock until smooth before it goes in the pot — added dry it will seize into lumps.

steps.heading: Simmer
steps.description: Combine everything and simmer gently until the oil floats. Stir often; groundnut catches easily.

steps.heading: Greens
steps.description: Stir in the spinach and turn off the heat.

name: Ofe Onugbu (Bitterleaf Soup)
whatMakesItGood: How much you wash the bitter leaf decides the whole dish. Washed too little it is inedible; washed too much it is just a green soup with no character.
description: Cocoyam-thickened soup with washed bitter leaf — bitter enough to notice, never enough to hurt.

steps.heading: Wash the leaves
steps.description: Wash the bitter leaf repeatedly, squeezing hard, until it tastes mildly bitter rather than sharp. Taste as you go — this is the whole recipe.

steps.heading: Boil the meats
steps.description: Cook the beef and stockfish with stock cubes until tender, keeping the stock.

steps.heading: Cocoyam paste
steps.description: Boil and pound the cocoyam smooth.

steps.heading: Thicken
steps.description: Drop the cocoyam into the boiling stock in lumps, cover, and let it dissolve before stirring.

steps.heading: Bring it together
steps.description: Add palm oil, crayfish, iru, pepper, dried fish and the washed bitter leaf. Simmer five minutes and check the salt.

name: Nigerian Beef Stew
whatMakesItGood: Frying the blend until the oil separates is not optional; it is the difference between stew that keeps for a week and stew that sours in two days.
description: The base stew that lives in every fridge — fried pepper and tomato with beef, ready for rice, yam, beans or bread.

steps.heading: Season and boil the beef
steps.description: Boil the beef with onion, thyme, one stock cube and salt until tender. Keep the stock.

steps.heading: Fry the beef
steps.description: Lift the meat out and fry it briefly in a little oil to seal it. Set aside.

steps.heading: Blend and reduce
steps.description: Blend the tomatoes, tatashe, pepper and one onion, then boil the blend down in a dry pot until the water is gone.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry the reduced blend in the hot oil with the tomato paste until the oil rises clear to the top. This takes longer than you think.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Return the beef and some stock, season, and simmer until it is the thickness you want.

name: Native Jollof (Palm Oil Jollof)
whatMakesItGood: Most people meet jollof as the party version. This is the one that came first — palm oil and locust bean give it a depth tomato alone never reaches.
description: Jollof built on palm oil, iru and dried fish instead of tomato paste and vegetable oil. Darker, smokier, older.

steps.heading: Parboil the rice
steps.description: Parboil the rice for eight minutes, rinse well, and drain. Rinsing is what stops it going sticky.

steps.heading: Start the base
steps.description: Heat the palm oil, add chopped onion, ground pepper, iru and crayfish, and fry until fragrant.

steps.heading: Add the proteins
steps.description: Stir in the dried fish and ponmo with a little stock, and let everything cook together.

steps.heading: Cook the rice
steps.description: Add the rice and just enough stock to cover. Cover tightly and cook on low — do not stir until the water is nearly gone.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Fold the ugu through, cover for two minutes off the heat, and serve.

name: Coconut Jollof Rice
whatMakesItGood: The coconut milk replaces the stock, not the pepper base, so it stays recognisably jollof. Watch the salt; coconut milk needs more than you expect.
description: Jollof cooked in coconut milk instead of stock — sweeter, softer, and a different dish entirely from coconut rice.

steps.heading: Parboil
steps.description: Parboil and rinse the rice, then drain it well.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Blend the tomatoes, tatashe, pepper and onion. Reduce, then fry in oil with the tomato paste until the oil separates.

steps.heading: Add coconut
steps.description: Pour in the coconut milk, season with thyme, curry and stock cubes, and bring it to a simmer.

steps.heading: Cook
steps.description: Stir the rice in, cover tightly, and cook on the lowest heat until the liquid is absorbed. Do not lift the lid too often.

steps.heading: Rest
steps.description: Turn off the heat and leave it covered for five minutes before fluffing.

name: Palm Oil Rice (Iwuk Edesi)
whatMakesItGood: Cooked wetter than jollof on purpose. The rice absorbs the seafood stock, which is why so little meat goes a long way.
description: Efik one-pot rice with palm oil, periwinkle and greens — closer to a wet rice than a fried one.

steps.heading: Parboil the rice
steps.description: Parboil the rice briefly and rinse.

steps.heading: Build the pot
steps.description: Heat palm oil, add onion, ground pepper and crayfish, and fry until it smells right.

steps.heading: Add proteins
steps.description: Add the dried fish, periwinkle and stock cubes with water, and let it boil into a proper broth.

steps.heading: Cook the rice
steps.description: Add the rice, cover, and cook on low until soft. It should stay a little wet.

steps.heading: Greens
steps.description: Stir in the ugu at the very end and cover for two minutes.

name: Tuwo Shinkafa
whatMakesItGood: Made from soft, broken rice rather than long grain — using the wrong rice gives you grains instead of a smooth swallow.
description: Soft rice swallow from the north, pounded smooth and served with miyan kuka or miyan taushe.

steps.heading: Overcook the rice
steps.description: Boil the rice with plenty of water until it is far past done and completely broken down.

steps.heading: Mash
steps.description: Mash it against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon until no whole grains are left.

steps.heading: Bring together
steps.description: Keep stirring over low heat until it pulls away from the pot as one soft mass.

steps.heading: Shape
steps.description: Wet a bowl, scoop portions in, and turn them out into rounds.

name: Tuwo Masara
whatMakesItGood: Corn flour behaves differently from cassava — it needs a slurry first or it seizes into lumps that never come out.
description: Maize swallow, softer and sweeter than rice tuwo, eaten with kuka or okra soup.

steps.heading: Make a slurry
steps.description: Mix a third of the corn flour with cold water until smooth. Cold water first, always.

steps.heading: Boil
steps.description: Bring the rest of the water to a boil, then stir the slurry in and cook until it thickens.

steps.heading: Add the rest
steps.description: Sprinkle in the remaining flour while stirring hard against the side of the pot.

steps.heading: Steam
steps.description: Cover on the lowest heat for five minutes, then stir once more and shape.

name: Amala and Ewedu
whatMakesItGood: Amala needs boiling water and fast stirring; hesitate and you get lumps you cannot beat out. The ewedu broom whisk exists for a reason.
description: Yam flour swallow with jute leaf soup — the Ibadan plate, usually with a spoon of gbegiri and stew beside it.

steps.heading: Boil the ewedu
steps.description: Boil the ewedu leaves with a little water, iru and stock cube until soft.

steps.heading: Whisk
steps.description: Whisk or blend briefly until it draws. Do not over-blend or it turns to pulp.

steps.heading: Make the amala
steps.description: Pour the yam flour into boiling water in a steady stream while stirring hard and without stopping.

steps.heading: Turn it
steps.description: Keep turning until it is smooth, stiff and evenly brown, adding splashes of hot water if it is too tight.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Shape the amala and serve with the ewedu and a stew alongside.

name: Eba
whatMakesItGood: The ratio is the recipe. Too much garri and it is a rock, too little and it slumps. Add garri to water, never water to garri.
description: Garri turned in hot water — the fastest swallow there is, and the one most homes fall back on.

steps.heading: Boil
steps.description: Bring the water to a full rolling boil and take it off the heat.

steps.heading: Pour in the garri
steps.description: Sprinkle the garri in evenly and let it sit and absorb for thirty seconds before touching it.

steps.heading: Turn
steps.description: Turn firmly with a wooden spoon until smooth with no dry pockets.

name: Semo
whatMakesItGood: Semo takes on whatever soup you give it, which is why it suits a house where nobody agrees. Cook it two minutes longer than feels necessary to lose the raw taste.
description: Semolina swallow — mild, smooth, and the usual choice when everyone at the table wants something different.

steps.heading: Boil the water
steps.description: Bring the water to a rolling boil.

steps.heading: Add the semo
steps.description: Pour it in gradually while stirring continuously to keep it lump-free.

steps.heading: Cook it out
steps.description: Lower the heat, cover for three minutes, then turn again until smooth and glossy.

name: Pounded Yam
whatMakesItGood: No flour, no water, nothing but yam. The stretch comes from beating it while it is still too hot to touch comfortably, which is the part nobody enjoys.
description: Real pounded yam — boiled yam beaten until it is smooth and stretchy, with nothing added.

steps.heading: Prepare the yam
steps.description: Peel and cut the yam into rounds, then rinse to take off the surface starch.

steps.heading: Boil
steps.description: Boil until a knife goes through with no resistance at all. Undercooked yam will never pound smooth.

steps.heading: Pound
steps.description: Pound in a mortar while hot, in batches, until completely smooth and elastic.

steps.heading: Shape
steps.description: Wet your hands, shape into rounds, and serve straight away.

name: Cassava Fufu
whatMakesItGood: The sourness is the ferment doing its job and is meant to be there. Cook it long enough that the raw cassava smell has fully gone.
description: Fermented cassava swallow, soft and slightly sour, cooked from the wet paste.

steps.heading: Make a paste
steps.description: Mix the fufu flour with cold water into a smooth lump-free slurry.

steps.heading: Cook
steps.description: Pour into a pot over medium heat and stir constantly as it thickens.

steps.heading: Work it
steps.description: Keep turning as it stiffens, adding hot water if needed, until it is smooth and pulls cleanly from the pot.

steps.heading: Shape
steps.description: Mould into balls and wrap while warm.

name: Peppered Chicken
whatMakesItGood: Boiling the chicken in heavy seasoning before it ever meets oil is what gets flavour past the skin. Frying afterwards is only for texture.
description: Chicken boiled in its own seasoning, fried, then tossed in a thick pepper sauce until every piece is coated.

steps.heading: Season and boil
steps.description: Boil the chicken with onion, curry, thyme, ginger, garlic and stock cubes in very little water so the stock stays strong.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Drain well and fry the pieces until golden. Wet chicken will spit, so pat it dry first.

steps.heading: Make the sauce
steps.description: Blend the tatashe, scotch bonnet and remaining onion and fry in the same oil until thick and no longer raw.

steps.heading: Toss
steps.description: Return the chicken to the sauce with a splash of stock and turn until every piece is coated.

name: Asun (Peppered Goat)
whatMakesItGood: The smoke is not optional — asun grilled over charcoal and asun fried in a pan are two different foods. Cook the goat until properly tender first; the grill is only for colour.
description: Smoky grilled goat meat chopped small and tossed with onions and a lot of scotch bonnet.

steps.heading: Boil the goat
steps.description: Cook the goat with onion, curry, thyme, stock cubes and salt until fully tender.

steps.heading: Grill
steps.description: Grill or roast the pieces until the edges char. This is where the smoke comes from.

steps.heading: Chop
steps.description: Cut the meat into small bite-sized cubes.

steps.heading: Toss
steps.description: Fry the sliced onion and ground pepper briefly in oil, then toss the goat through off the heat so it stays juicy.

name: Nkwobi
whatMakesItGood: The palm oil is emulsified with potash until it turns pale and creamy — that chemistry is the entire dish, and it is why nkwobi does not look like palm oil at all.
description: Cow foot in a thick palm oil paste set with potash, served warm in a wooden bowl with utazi on top.

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Boil the cow foot with onion, stock cubes and salt until it is soft and gelatinous. This takes a long time — do not rush it.

steps.heading: Make the paste
steps.description: Dissolve a small piece of potash in water, strain it, and beat it into the palm oil until the oil thickens and turns pale yellow.

steps.heading: Season the paste
steps.description: Stir the ground pepper, crayfish and a stock cube into the paste.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Fold the warm meat through the paste until every piece is coated.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Top with thinly sliced utazi and sliced onion, and serve warm.

name: Isi Ewu
whatMakesItGood: Every part of the head has a different texture, which is the point. Same emulsified palm oil base as nkwobi, but the meat makes it a bigger dish.
description: Goat head in the same palm oil paste as nkwobi — richer, and traditionally the dish you serve a guest you respect.

steps.heading: Clean thoroughly
steps.description: Wash the goat head very well, scraping the skin. Any shortcut here shows up in the taste.

steps.heading: Boil
steps.description: Cook with onion, stock cubes and salt until tender, then pick the meat off in pieces.

steps.heading: Emulsify
steps.description: Beat strained potash water into the palm oil until it goes thick and pale.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Stir in ground pepper, ground ehu and a stock cube.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Fold the meat through, top with utazi and onion rings, and serve warm.

name: Designer Stew (Ofada Sauce)
whatMakesItGood: Made with unripe green peppers rather than red, and the oil is deliberately bleached first. That bleaching is what gives it the colour and the smell.
description: Green pepper stew bleached with a lot of oil, loaded with assorted meat and iru, served with ofada rice.

steps.heading: Cook the meats
steps.description: Boil the beef, ponmo and shaki together with stock cubes and onion until tender. Keep the stock.

steps.heading: Blend and drain
steps.description: Blend the green peppers, scotch bonnet and onion coarsely, then drain off as much water as you can.

steps.heading: Bleach the oil
steps.description: Heat the palm oil until it turns clear and smokes, then take it off carefully. Open a window first.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry the drained pepper blend with the iru in the bleached oil until it darkens and the oil separates.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add the meats and stock, simmer, and lay boiled eggs on top before serving with ofada rice.

name: Egg Sauce
whatMakesItGood: The eggs go in last and barely cook. Stirring them into a hot base for too long turns the whole thing dry and grey.
description: Eggs scrambled into a fried pepper and tomato base — the standard partner for boiled yam or plantain.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry the chopped onion, tomato and pepper in oil until the tomato breaks down and loses its raw edge.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Add the stock cube and salt and let the sauce thicken.

steps.heading: Add the eggs
steps.description: Beat the eggs and pour them in, stirring slowly so they set in soft folds rather than fine crumbs.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Take it off while the eggs still look slightly wet — they carry on cooking in the pan.

name: Nigerian Fried Fish
whatMakesItGood: Dry the fish properly and score it to the bone so the seasoning gets in. Wet fish steams instead of frying and the skin never crisps.
description: Titus or mackerel seasoned hard, then fried until the skin crisps — the fish that sits on top of everything.

steps.heading: Clean and score
steps.description: Gut and wash the fish, then cut two or three deep slashes into each side.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Rub in blended onion, ginger, curry, thyme, stock cubes and salt, and leave it for at least twenty minutes.

steps.heading: Dry
steps.description: Pat the surface dry before it goes near the oil.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Fry in hot oil without moving it until the underside releases on its own, then turn once.

steps.heading: Drain
steps.description: Rest on a rack, not on paper, so the bottom stays crisp.

name: Point and Kill Catfish
whatMakesItGood: There is nowhere for a tired fish to hide in this broth, which is why it is ordered live. Wash with hot water to firm the skin so it holds together.
description: Fresh catfish in a clear, fiercely peppered broth — no oil, no thickener, nothing to hide behind.

steps.heading: Prepare the fish
steps.description: Wash the cut catfish in hot water with salt to remove the slime and firm the skin.

steps.heading: Build the broth
steps.description: Boil water with the pepper soup spice, ground pepper, onion, uda and stock cubes for ten minutes before the fish goes in.

steps.heading: Cook the fish
steps.description: Add the fish and simmer gently. Never stir — shake the pot instead or it falls apart.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Drop in the scent leaf, check the salt, and take it off immediately.

name: Gizdodo with Gizzard
whatMakesItGood: Fry the plantain and gizzard separately and combine them at the very end, or the plantain goes soft and disappears into the sauce.
description: Fried plantain and gizzard folded into a thick pepper sauce — the small chops plate that eats like a meal.

steps.heading: Cook the gizzard
steps.description: Boil the gizzard with curry, stock cubes and onion until tender, then cut into bite-sized pieces.

steps.heading: Fry separately
steps.description: Fry the plantain cubes until golden and drain. Fry the gizzard until it browns at the edges.

steps.heading: Make the sauce
steps.description: Blend and fry the peppers and onion until thick and the oil separates.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Fold the gizzard through the sauce first, then the plantain, off the heat.

name: Chicken Pepper Soup
whatMakesItGood: It works because it is thin. No oil, no thickener; just spice, heat and good stock, which is why it feels medicinal in the best way.
description: Clear, hot broth with chicken and pepper soup spice — the thing you cook for someone with a cold.

steps.heading: Season the chicken
steps.description: Put the chicken in a pot with onion, ginger, stock cubes and salt, and let it sweat for five minutes before adding water.

steps.heading: Simmer
steps.description: Add water to just cover and simmer until the chicken is tender.

steps.heading: Spice it
steps.description: Stir in the pepper soup spice and ground scotch bonnet and cook another ten minutes so the spice opens up.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add scent leaf, taste for salt, and serve very hot.

name: Pap and Akara
whatMakesItGood: Pap must be made with boiling water poured fast onto a cold slurry. Lukewarm water gives you a raw, chalky bowl that no amount of sugar rescues.
description: Smooth fermented corn pap with bean cakes — the breakfast that has fed more Nigerian mornings than anything else.

steps.heading: Peel the beans
steps.description: Soak the beans, rub off the skins, and rinse until clean.

steps.heading: Blend
steps.description: Blend the peeled beans with the onion and pepper using as little water as possible, then whisk hard to get air in.

steps.heading: Fry the akara
steps.description: Scoop into hot oil and fry until golden and puffed. Crowding the pot makes them flat.

steps.heading: Make the pap
steps.description: Mix the pap with cold water into a smooth slurry, then pour boiling water in quickly while stirring until it thickens and turns glossy.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Sweeten the pap to taste and serve hot with the akara.

name: Custard
whatMakesItGood: Same technique as pap: cold slurry first, then boiling water in one go. Poured slowly it lumps and never recovers.
description: Smooth custard whisked with boiling water, sweetened and taken with milk — the quick morning drink.

steps.heading: Slurry
steps.description: Mix the custard powder with a little cold water until completely smooth.

steps.heading: Add boiling water
steps.description: Pour freshly boiled water in quickly while stirring hard, until it thickens and turns glossy.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Stir in the sugar and milk and serve hot.

name: Puff Puff
whatMakesItGood: The batter should be thick enough to hold on a spoon but loose enough to drop. Too stiff and you get bread; too loose and it spreads flat in the oil.
description: Sweet yeasted dough balls fried until deep brown — soft inside, slightly chewy, gone in minutes.

steps.heading: Activate the yeast
steps.description: Mix the yeast and a spoon of sugar into warm — not hot — water and leave it until it froths.

steps.heading: Make the batter
steps.description: Combine the flour, sugar, nutmeg and salt, then stir the yeast water in to a thick, sticky batter.

steps.heading: Prove
steps.description: Cover and leave somewhere warm until it has doubled and smells yeasty.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Drop spoonfuls into medium-hot oil. Too hot and they brown before the middle cooks.

name: Chin Chin
whatMakesItGood: Rest the dough before cutting or it shrinks and toughens. Fry at a moderate heat so the inside dries out and it stays crunchy for days.
description: Crunchy fried dough cubes — the tin on top of the fridge that never lasts a week.

steps.heading: Rub in
steps.description: Rub the butter into the flour, sugar, milk, nutmeg, baking powder and salt until it looks like breadcrumbs.

steps.heading: Bind
steps.description: Work in the beaten eggs and just enough water to bring it into a firm dough.

steps.heading: Rest
steps.description: Cover and rest the dough for fifteen minutes.

steps.heading: Roll and cut
steps.description: Roll out thin and cut into small squares.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Fry in batches at a moderate heat until evenly golden, then drain and cool completely before storing.

name: Nigerian Meat Pie
whatMakesItGood: The filling must be cold and thick before it goes in the pastry. Warm, wet filling steams the crust from inside and the bottom goes soggy.
description: Thick shortcrust filled with minced beef, potato and carrot in a set gravy.

steps.heading: Make the pastry
steps.description: Rub the cold butter into the flour and salt, then bind with cold water into a firm dough. Chill it.

steps.heading: Cook the filling
steps.description: Fry the onion and mince, add diced potato and carrot, thyme, stock cubes and a little water, and cook until soft.

steps.heading: Thicken and cool
steps.description: Stir in cornstarch slaked in water to set the gravy, then cool the filling completely.

steps.heading: Assemble
steps.description: Roll the pastry, cut rounds, fill, fold and seal the edges firmly with a fork.

steps.heading: Bake
steps.description: Brush with egg and bake at 180C until deep golden.

name: Nigerian Buns
whatMakesItGood: Buns use baking powder rather than yeast, so there is no waiting. The batter must be stiff — that density is the whole difference from puff puff.
description: Dense, slightly sweet fried dough balls — heavier and crunchier than puff puff, and no yeast involved.

steps.heading: Mix dry
steps.description: Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, nutmeg and salt.

steps.heading: Bind
steps.description: Work in the butter, egg and enough water to make a thick, stiff batter that holds its shape.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Drop rough balls into medium-hot oil and fry until deep brown all over.

steps.heading: Drain
steps.description: Lift out and drain well.

name: Boli and Groundnut
whatMakesItGood: Use plantain that is ripe but still firm. Fully soft plantain collapses on the grill and turns to sugar before the inside heats through.
description: Roasted plantain with roasted groundnuts — the roadside pairing that needs no pot at all.

steps.heading: Prepare
steps.description: Peel the plantains and leave them whole or halve them lengthways.

steps.heading: Roast
steps.description: Roast over charcoal or in a hot oven, turning often, until they blister and char in patches.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Serve hot with the groundnuts, and a little pepper-salted palm oil for dipping if you want it.

name: Yam and Vegetable Porridge
whatMakesItGood: Some of the yam is meant to dissolve — that is what thickens it. Cut the pieces unevenly on purpose so part collapses and part holds.
description: Yam simmered until it breaks down into its own sauce, with palm oil and greens stirred through.

steps.heading: Prepare the yam
steps.description: Peel and cut the yam into rough chunks of different sizes, then rinse.

steps.heading: Boil
steps.description: Cook with just enough water to cover, along with the blended pepper, onion and tomato.

steps.heading: Enrich
steps.description: Stir in the palm oil, crayfish, dried fish and stock cubes, mashing some of the yam against the pot to thicken it.

steps.heading: Greens
steps.description: Fold the ugu through and turn off the heat.

name: Beans Porridge
whatMakesItGood: Never salt beans until they are already soft — salt early and the skins toughen and they take twice as long.
description: Brown beans cooked until soft and creamy with palm oil, pepper and onion.

steps.heading: Wash and boil
steps.description: Rinse the beans and boil in plenty of unsalted water until the skins begin to soften.

steps.heading: Top up
steps.description: Keep adding hot — never cold — water as it reduces. Cold water shocks the beans and slows everything down.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Once soft, add the palm oil, blended pepper, onion, crayfish and stock cubes.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Simmer until thick and creamy, then salt to taste.

name: Akara
whatMakesItGood: Whisking air into the batter is what makes it float and puff. A dense akara means it was blended with too much water or not beaten enough.
description: Bean cakes fried until puffed and golden — crisp outside, airy inside.

steps.heading: Soak and peel
steps.description: Soak the beans for an hour, then rub between your palms until every skin floats off.

steps.heading: Blend thick
steps.description: Blend with the onion and pepper using the least water you can manage.

steps.heading: Whisk
steps.description: Beat the batter hard with a wooden spoon until it lightens and holds air.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Scoop into hot oil and fry until golden on both sides, turning once.

name: Miyan Kuka
whatMakesItGood: Kuka powder is sifted in at the end, never boiled hard, or it turns bitter and loses the draw entirely.
description: Baobab leaf powder soup, dark and drawing, eaten with tuwo across the north.

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Boil the beef with onion, stock cubes and salt until tender, keeping the stock.

steps.heading: Season the stock
steps.description: Add the dry pepper, crayfish, iru, dried fish and oil to the stock and simmer.

steps.heading: Add the kuka
steps.description: Sift the baobab powder in slowly while stirring so it does not clump, then simmer very briefly.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Check the salt and serve with tuwo.

name: Miyan Taushe
whatMakesItGood: The pumpkin is cooked until it collapses and becomes the body of the soup. Groundnut paste rounds it out so the sweetness does not take over.
description: Pumpkin soup with groundnut paste and spinach — thick, mildly sweet, and a northern staple.

steps.heading: Boil the beef
steps.description: Cook the beef with onion and stock cubes until tender. Keep the stock.

steps.heading: Cook the pumpkin
steps.description: Boil the peeled pumpkin until completely soft, then mash it smooth.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry the blended tomato, pepper and onion until the raw smell goes.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add the pumpkin, loosened groundnut paste and stock, and simmer until thick.

steps.heading: Greens
steps.description: Stir the spinach in at the end.

name: Dan Wake
whatMakesItGood: The dough must be firm enough to hold as dumplings in boiling water. A little potash keeps them from breaking apart.
description: Bean flour dumplings boiled and tossed with oil, pepper and onion — northern street food.

steps.heading: Make the dough
steps.description: Mix the bean flour and plain flour with warm water and salt into a firm dough.

steps.heading: Shape
steps.description: Roll into small balls or short ropes.

steps.heading: Boil
steps.description: Drop into boiling water and cook until they float and firm up.

steps.heading: Toss
steps.description: Drain and toss with oil, dry pepper, sliced onion, crushed groundnuts and stock cube.

name: Masa
whatMakesItGood: The batter is fermented, which is where the sourness and the lift come from. Skip the rest and you get flat rice pancakes instead.
description: Fermented rice cakes, soft and slightly sour, cooked in a dimpled pan and eaten with soup or honey.

steps.heading: Soak the rice
steps.description: Soak the rice for several hours, then drain.

steps.heading: Blend
steps.description: Blend most of the rice with a little water into a thick batter, cooking a small portion first and blending it in to help the texture.

steps.heading: Ferment
steps.description: Add the yeast and sugar and leave the batter somewhere warm until it rises and smells sour.

steps.heading: Cook
steps.description: Salt the batter, then cook spoonfuls in a greased dimpled pan, turning once, until golden on both sides.

name: Kilishi
whatMakesItGood: It keeps for weeks without a fridge because it is dried right down. The groundnut coating is what separates it from ordinary dried meat.
description: Beef sliced paper-thin, coated in a spiced groundnut paste and dried until it snaps.

steps.heading: Slice thin
steps.description: Slice the beef along the grain as thinly as you possibly can — thickness decides whether it dries or spoils.

steps.heading: First dry
steps.description: Lay the slices out in the sun or a low oven until they are leathery.

steps.heading: Make the paste
steps.description: Blend the groundnut paste with pepper, ginger, garlic, onion, stock cubes and water into a thin coating.

steps.heading: Soak
steps.description: Dip each slice in the paste and lay it back out.

steps.heading: Second dry
steps.description: Dry again completely, then finish briefly over open heat for the smoke.

name: Zobo
whatMakesItGood: Do not boil the petals for long. A short steep gives you colour and brightness; a long boil turns it flat and stewed.
description: Hibiscus steeped with ginger, pineapple and cloves, then chilled — deep red and sharp.

steps.heading: Rinse
steps.description: Rinse the zobo leaves to wash off dust and grit.

steps.heading: Steep
steps.description: Bring the water to a boil, add the leaves, ginger, pineapple skins and cloves, and steep off the heat.

steps.heading: Strain
steps.description: Strain out all the solids and press to get everything through.

steps.heading: Sweeten and chill
steps.description: Sweeten to taste, add lemon and pineapple juice, and chill thoroughly before serving.

name: Kunu Aya (Tigernut Drink)
whatMakesItGood: Soaking the tigernuts long enough is what makes them blend smooth. Rushed, the drink is gritty no matter how fine your sieve is.
description: Tigernuts blended with dates and coconut into a creamy, naturally sweet drink.

steps.heading: Soak
steps.description: Soak the tigernuts overnight, or at least four hours, until they soften.

steps.heading: Blend
steps.description: Blend with the dates, coconut, ginger and water until as smooth as it will go.

steps.heading: Sieve
steps.description: Strain through a fine cloth, squeezing hard to get all the milk out.

steps.heading: Chill
steps.description: Chill and shake before serving; it separates naturally.

name: Chapman
whatMakesItGood: A few drops of bitters is what makes it a chapman rather than mixed soft drinks. Add it last and taste as you go.
description: The Nigerian bar drink — Fanta, Sprite, blackcurrant and bitters over ice with cucumber.

steps.heading: Prepare
steps.description: Slice the cucumber, lemon and orange thinly.

steps.heading: Build
steps.description: Fill a jug with ice, add the fruit slices, and pour in the soft drinks and blackcurrant.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add a few drops of bitters, stir once, and serve immediately while cold.

name: Beef Suya Skewers
whatMakesItGood: Half the yaji goes on before grilling and half after. The second dusting is the one you actually taste, because grilling burns off the first.
description: Thin beef coated in yaji spice and grilled over open heat, served with raw onion and more spice.

steps.heading: Make the yaji
steps.description: Grind the roasted groundnuts to a coarse powder and mix with dry pepper, ginger, garlic powder, stock cubes and salt.

steps.heading: Slice the beef
steps.description: Cut the beef into very thin wide strips against the grain.

steps.heading: Coat
steps.description: Toss the strips in oil, then in half the yaji, and leave to sit.

steps.heading: Grill
steps.description: Thread onto skewers and grill over high heat, turning, until the edges char.

steps.heading: Dust
steps.description: Dust with the remaining yaji off the heat and serve with sliced raw onion.

name: Abacha (African Salad)
whatMakesItGood: Served at room temperature, not hot. The palm oil is worked with potash until it turns yellow and creamy, which is what binds the whole salad.
description: Shredded dried cassava soaked soft and dressed in emulsified palm oil with potash, ponmo and garden egg leaf.

steps.heading: Soak the abacha
steps.description: Soak the dried shredded cassava in warm water until soft, then drain thoroughly.

steps.heading: Cook the ponmo
steps.description: Boil the ponmo with a stock cube until tender and cut into strips.

steps.heading: Make the sauce
steps.description: Beat strained potash water into the palm oil until it thickens and turns pale, then season with crayfish, pepper and stock cube.

steps.heading: Toss
steps.description: Fold the drained abacha and ponmo through the sauce until evenly coated.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Top with shredded garden egg leaf and sliced onion and serve at room temperature.

name: Macaroni Jollof
whatMakesItGood: Cooking the pasta in the sauce instead of draining it is what makes this jollof rather than pasta with stew. Use less liquid than you think.
description: Macaroni cooked straight in the stew base rather than boiled separately, so it takes the colour all through.

steps.heading: Make the base
steps.description: Blend the tomatoes, tatashe, pepper and onion, reduce, then fry in oil with the tomato paste until the oil separates.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Add curry, thyme, stock cubes and enough water to just cover the pasta you are about to add.

steps.heading: Cook the pasta
steps.description: Stir in the dry macaroni, cover, and cook on low, checking that it does not catch.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Turn off while there is still a little sauce clinging — it keeps absorbing off the heat.

name: Nigerian Spaghetti Stir Fry
whatMakesItGood: Undercook the spaghetti by two minutes before it hits the pan, or it turns to mush during the toss.
description: Boiled spaghetti tossed hard in a hot pan with vegetables, sausage and curry.

steps.heading: Boil the pasta
steps.description: Cook the spaghetti two minutes short of done, drain, and toss with a little oil.

steps.heading: Prep the vegetables
steps.description: Slice the carrots, beans and cabbage thinly and evenly so they cook at the same rate.

steps.heading: Stir fry
steps.description: Fry the onion, pepper and sausage on high heat, then add the vegetables and keep them moving.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add the spaghetti, curry and stock cubes and toss hard until everything is coated and hot.

name: Boiled Yam and Egg Sauce
whatMakesItGood: Salt the yam water properly — yam boiled in plain water tastes of nothing and no sauce can fix that afterwards.
description: Plain boiled yam with a loose, peppery egg sauce poured over it.

steps.heading: Boil the yam
steps.description: Peel, cut and boil the yam in well-salted water until a knife slides in easily.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry the chopped onion, tomato and pepper in oil until thick.

steps.heading: Add the eggs
steps.description: Beat and pour in the eggs, folding gently so they stay in soft curds.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Season and spoon over the drained hot yam.

name: Fried Plantain and Egg
whatMakesItGood: Ripe plantain browns fast because of the sugar. Medium heat, not high, or it burns black outside while raw inside.
description: Dodo with a folded pepper omelette — the quickest full meal in the house.

steps.heading: Fry the plantain
steps.description: Slice and fry the plantain on medium heat until golden on both sides, then drain.

steps.heading: Make the omelette
steps.description: Beat the eggs with chopped onion, pepper, tomato and salt.

steps.heading: Cook
steps.description: Pour into the hot pan, let the base set, then fold over and cook through.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Serve together while both are still hot.

name: Indomie and Egg
whatMakesItGood: Use less water than the pack says and add the seasoning at the end. Boiled in the full amount, it comes out as soup rather than noodles.
description: Instant noodles upgraded with fresh pepper, onion and a fried egg on top.

steps.heading: Boil short
steps.description: Boil the noodles in a small amount of water for three minutes and drain almost dry.

steps.heading: Fry the vegetables
steps.description: Fry the onion, pepper and carrot briefly in oil.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add the noodles and seasoning sachets and toss on high heat.

steps.heading: Top
steps.description: Fry the eggs separately and lay them on top.

name: Boiled Corn and Ube
whatMakesItGood: The pear only needs warm water to go soft and buttery. Boiling it hard turns it bitter and slippery.
description: Fresh corn boiled and eaten with softened African pear — a season, not a recipe.

steps.heading: Boil the corn
steps.description: Boil the corn in salted water until the kernels are tender but still have bite.

steps.heading: Soften the ube
steps.description: Pour hot water over the ube in a covered bowl and leave for five minutes until it softens.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.description: Drain both and eat together while warm.

name: Ewa Riro
whatMakesItGood: Unlike ewa agoyin, the sauce is stirred through rather than served on top, so every spoon is the same.
description: Beans cooked soft then stirred into a fried pepper base — richer and more seasoned than plain porridge.

steps.heading: Boil the beans
steps.description: Cook the beans in unsalted water until completely soft, topping up with hot water.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Blend the peppers and onion and fry in palm oil until reduced and the oil separates.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Stir the fried base into the beans with crayfish and stock cubes.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Simmer together, mash slightly for body, and salt to taste.

name: Frejon
whatMakesItGood: Eaten once a year in a lot of Lagos homes, with garri and fish stew on the side. The beans are sieved smooth, which is what separates it from porridge.
description: Black beans blended with coconut milk into a smooth sweet soup — the Lagos Good Friday dish.

steps.heading: Boil the beans
steps.description: Cook the beans until they collapse completely.

steps.heading: Blend
steps.description: Blend the beans with their liquid until smooth, then sieve out the skins.

steps.heading: Add coconut
steps.description: Return to the pot with the coconut milk and cloves and simmer gently.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Sweeten lightly, season with salt, and serve with garri.

name: Okra Soup with Assorted Meat
whatMakesItGood: Okra loses its draw the longer it cooks. Five minutes is plenty — anything more and you have green soup with no pull at all.
description: Chopped okra cooked briefly so it keeps its draw, with assorted meat and palm oil.

steps.heading: Cook the meats
steps.description: Boil the beef, ponmo and shaki with stock cubes and onion until tender.

steps.heading: Prepare the okra
steps.description: Chop or grate the okra. Chopped gives you bite, grated gives you more draw.

steps.heading: Build
steps.description: Add palm oil, crayfish, ground pepper and dried fish to the meat stock and bring to a boil.

steps.heading: Add okra
steps.description: Stir the okra in and cook no more than five minutes.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Fold in the ugu and take it straight off the heat.

name: Goat Meat White Soup
whatMakesItGood: Goat needs far longer than catfish, so the yam thickener goes in only once the meat is genuinely tender, not before.
description: Nsala made with goat instead of fish — heavier, and the version cooked for guests.

steps.heading: Boil the goat
steps.description: Cook the goat with onion, uda, stock cubes and salt until properly tender.

steps.heading: Yam paste
steps.description: Boil the yam separately until soft and pound it smooth with a little water.

steps.heading: Thicken
steps.description: Drop the yam paste into the simmering stock in small lumps and let them dissolve without stirring hard.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add crayfish, ground pepper, uziza and utazi, and cook two minutes more.

name: Miyan Agushi
whatMakesItGood: Ground melon is stirred into the stock as a paste rather than fried in lumps, which is why it comes out smooth instead of caked.
description: Northern melon seed soup — smoother and thinner than Igbo egusi, with spinach through it.

steps.heading: Cook the beef
steps.description: Boil the beef with onion and stock cubes until tender, keeping the stock.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Fry the blended tomato, onion and pepper in oil until the water goes.

steps.heading: Add the melon
steps.description: Mix the ground egusi with a little stock into a paste and stir it into the pot.

steps.heading: Simmer
steps.description: Cook gently until the oil rises, stirring so it does not catch.

steps.heading: Greens
steps.description: Stir in the spinach and turn off.

name: Ila Alasepo
whatMakesItGood: Alasepo means cooked together. The okra goes into the stew itself, so it takes the pepper right through instead of sitting in it.
description: Okra cooked together with the stew rather than beside it — one pot, red and drawing.

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Boil the beef with stock cubes and onion until tender.

steps.heading: Fry the base
steps.description: Blend the peppers and tomato and fry in palm oil until reduced.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add stock, crayfish and dried fish and let it simmer into a proper stew.

steps.heading: Add okra
steps.description: Stir the chopped okra in and cook only five minutes so it keeps its draw.

name: Efo Elegusi
whatMakesItGood: The lumps are deliberate. Frying the egusi paste undisturbed until it sets is what gives you those curds instead of a smooth sauce.
description: Egusi and spinach cooked the Yoruba way — the melon left in visible lumps rather than dissolved.

steps.heading: Cook the meats
steps.description: Boil the beef and ponmo with stock cubes until tender, keeping the stock.

steps.heading: Fry the pepper
steps.description: Fry the blended pepper in palm oil until the oil separates.

steps.heading: Add the egusi
steps.description: Mix the ground egusi with a little water and drop it in as lumps. Leave it alone to set before stirring.

steps.heading: Simmer
steps.description: Add stock, crayfish, iru and dried fish and simmer until the oil floats.

steps.heading: Greens
steps.description: Stir the shoko through and take it off.

name: Ayamase
whatMakesItGood: Ayamase is defined by the bleached oil and the green pepper. Using red pepper makes it an ordinary stew with a different name.
description: The green pepper stew proper — bleached palm oil, iru and assorted meat, served with ofada rice.

steps.heading: Boil the meat
steps.description: Cook the beef and ponmo with stock cubes and onion until tender.

steps.heading: Drain the blend
steps.description: Blend the green peppers and scotch bonnet coarsely and drain off the water thoroughly.

steps.heading: Bleach the oil
steps.description: Heat the palm oil until it clears and smokes, then cool it slightly. Ventilate the kitchen.

steps.heading: Fry
steps.description: Fry the pepper blend and iru in the oil until it darkens and thickens.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Add the meats and stock, simmer, and serve with boiled eggs on top.

name: Ogbono Soup
whatMakesItGood: Dissolve the ogbono in warm oil off the heat before it meets water. Thrown straight into the pot it clumps and never draws properly.
description: Wild mango seed soup, thick and drawing, with assorted meat and a handful of greens.

steps.heading: Cook the meat
steps.description: Boil the beef and stockfish with stock cubes until tender, keeping the stock.

steps.heading: Dissolve
steps.description: Warm the palm oil, take it off the heat, and stir the ground ogbono in until smooth.

steps.heading: Combine
steps.description: Add the paste to the boiling stock, stirring, and let it draw for five minutes.

steps.heading: Season
steps.description: Add crayfish, pepper and dried fish and simmer.

steps.heading: Finish
steps.description: Stir in the ugu and serve.

name: Afang Soup
whatMakesItGood: Afang leaf is tough and must be pounded or very finely shredded. Waterleaf supplies all the moisture, so almost no water is added.
description: Shredded afang leaf with waterleaf, palm oil and plenty of assorted meat.

steps.heading: Cook the meats
steps.description: Boil the beef, ponmo and stockfish with stock cubes until tender and reduce the stock right down.

steps.heading: Prepare the afang
steps.description: Pound or finely shred the afang leaves — they will not soften on their own.

steps.heading: Build
steps.description: Add palm oil, crayfish, ground pepper and dried fish to the reduced stock.

steps.heading: Waterleaf
steps.description: Stir in the waterleaf and let its liquid cook off.

steps.heading: Afang last
steps.description: Add the afang and periwinkle, cover for four minutes, and turn off.

name: Egusi Soup
whatMakesItGood: Fry the egusi long enough that the raw seed smell is gone. Undercooked egusi tastes chalky no matter how well the rest is seasoned.
description: Ground melon seed soup with bitter leaf, palm oil and assorted meat.

steps.heading: Cook the meats
steps.description: Boil the beef and stockfish with stock cubes and onion until tender.

steps.heading: Fry the egusi
steps.description: Heat the palm oil, add the ground egusi mixed with a little water, and fry until it caks and the raw smell goes.
